by CEF Admin
on September 23, 2026

Johannesburg – The Central Energy Fund (CEF) Group today presented its five-year financial performance, governance outcomes, operational progress and strategic priorities to Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Mineral and Petroleum Resources.

The presentation covered the financial sustainability of iGas and the Strategic Fuel Fund (SFF), the financial and operational challenges facing PetroSA, progress in the operationalisation of the South African National Petroleum Company (SANPC), and the latest prefeasibility work on the redevelopment of the SANPC refinery.

The presentation comes against a challenging operating environment characterised by geopolitical instability, oil-price volatility, supply-chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and increased pressure on the domestic petroleum-products market.

CEF’s response is centred on commercial sustainability, operational stabilisation, portfolio and revenue diversification, accelerated execution and the responsible operationalisation of SANPC.

CEF Group: Stabilization, Growth and Value Realization

CEF Group CEO Dr Tshepo Mokoka said the five-year performance demonstrates both the resilience of parts of the portfolio and the need for decisive action to address legacy constraints and accelerate sustainable value creation.

“Our focus is to stabilise the operating entities, strengthen execution capability, diversify revenue streams and accelerate the operationalisation of SANPC. The objective is to ensure that the Group’s assets, capabilities and strategic mandate are translated into sustainable value and strengthened energy security for South Africa.”

iGas: Sustained Profitability and a Strengthened Financial Position

iGas recorded cumulative net profits of approximately R4.2 billion over the five-year period. Annual net profit increased by 143%, from R408.4 million in FY2021/22 to R993.5 million in FY2025/26, supported by increased equity-accounted income following the acquisition of an additional 15% interest in ROMPCO and interest income.

  • Total assets: R6.2 billion.
  • Shareholder equity: R5.5 billion.
  • Closing cash balance: R1.53 billion.
  • Return on equity: 18.17%.
  • Debt-to-equity: improved from 43% in FY2022/23 to 17% in FY2025/26.
  • Cash ratio: 2.33 in FY2025/26.

iGas’s free cash flow was R137 million in FY2025/26, following higher dividends paid to CEF SOC to support PetroSA. The company nevertheless remained an important contributor to the Group’s financial resilience.

SFF: Strong Balance Sheet Supporting the SANPC Transition

The Strategic Fuel Fund maintained a strong liquidity and solvency position during a period characterised by strategic stock transactions, infrastructure acquisitions and the operationalisation of SANPC.

  • FY2025/26 total assets: R10.4 billion.
  • Total equity: R9.0 billion.
  • Cash and cash equivalents: R5.19 billion.
  • Liquidity ratio: 24.97; solvency ratio: 7.59.
  • Average cash balances of R5 billion over the review period.

During the period, SFF paid approximately R2.3 billion following the Constitutional Court judgment relating to strategic stock transactions and approximately R2 billion to National Treasury. It also acquired interests in the Montague Terminal and Avedia Energy before transferring or assigning strategic assets and personnel as part of SANPC’s operationalisation.

Governance, Investigations and Consequence Management

CEF reported on governance and investigation matters associated with the legacy entities. In relation to SFF, internal processes relating to the strategic stock matter have been concluded, while the Hawks investigation remains ongoing.

A contingent liability relating to a potential Natixis claim of approximately US$23 million remains disclosed in the financial statements, subject to recovery efforts against third parties.

The internal forensic investigation into the Enviroshore matter was completed by Gobodo, with recommended criminal proceedings against relevant parties. The Zimbabwe/Line Petroleum internal investigation has also been concluded, with recovery efforts continuing in relation to proceeds from diesel transactions. CEF continues to strengthen consequence management, internal controls and corrective action.

PetroSA: Stabilization, Liquidity Management and Commercial Turnaround

PetroSA remains a strategically important national energy asset, but the five-year assessment confirms that the company continues to face significant financial, operational and liquidity pressures. The Mossel Bay Gas-to-Liquids (GTL) refinery and FA Platform have remained offline and on preservation mode since November 2020.

PetroSA has consequently relied on trading and importing refined petroleum products to generate cash, a model that produces lower margins than manufacturing and remains exposed to volatile product prices, supply conditions and funding requirements.

The five-year financial analysis shows that PetroSA reported losses in four of the last five financial years. The FY2022/23 profit was largely attributable to a revision in the abandonment provision/liability rather than an improvement in underlying operating performance.

Revenue levels have declined significantly, while gross margins have remained comparatively stable and have shown improvement as PetroSA works to expand its customer base. Other operating income, including landfill and insurance-related income, has also increased as the company pursues additional revenue streams.

Operating costs increased from approximately R2.2 billion to R3.5 billion over the period, reflecting labour, demurrage, maintenance and plant-preservation costs. Investment income has been earned from dividends and cash holdings, while finance costs have included the unwinding of interest on the abandonment liability, interest on the PetroSA Ghana FPSO lease and interest charged on late supplier payments.

PetroSA carries approximately R33 billion in assessed losses, meaning the PetroSA entity does not recognise an income-tax expense on those assessed losses; taxation in the reported results relates to PetroSA Ghana Limited.

Financial Position and Liquidity

The financial-position analysis in the presentation shows that PetroSA remains under severe strain. Capital expenditure has remained limited because the plant is on preservation mode, while portions of property, plant and equipment have been impaired.

The investment in PetroSA Ghana has reduced following impairment losses. Funds invested in the rehabilitation company are held for future decommissioning activities.

Inventory has reduced significantly as PetroSA has faced increasing difficulty securing cargoes on credit terms. Trade receivables have also declined, partly through non-payment and associated credit-loss provisions. At the same time, trade payables have risen as the company manages its working-capital cycle, with product suppliers constituting a significant component. Liquidity remains a major challenge and cash reserves have continued to decline.

The ratio analysis illustrates the pressure on the company: the current ratio declined from 1.74 in 2022 to 0.81 in 2025; the quick ratio declined from 1.47 to 0.76; and the cash ratio stood at 0.17 in 2025.

The presentation records negative debt-to-equity ratios, reflecting technical insolvency, while debt-to-assets remained above one. Profitability indicators also deteriorated, with return on capital employed and return on assets remaining negative in the latest year.

The presentation further notes that accounts payable materially exceed accounts receivable, contributing to the weak current ratio; operating expenditure remains too high for a trading business; and trading income alone is insufficient to support the current cost structure. Low cash balances constrain working capital available for cargo purchases.

Turnaround and Commercial Response

PetroSA is implementing a turnaround programme focused on cost containment, negotiated payment plans, portfolio diversification, stakeholder engagement, revenue diversification, market-share growth, finalisation of the GTL reinstatement assessment and partnership with SANPC.

The broader response also includes leveraging CEF Group shared services, improving execution capability and optimising the operating model. The company is targeting growth across State-Owned Enterprises, airlines, wholesale customers, independent and integrated oil companies, and strategic tender channels.

IOCs have signed monthly nominations for 12 months, except BP which has opted for a different supply arrangement. PetroSA has also secured the RT70 tender and has allocations from different State organs. SOE-to-SOE engagements are planned in line with the National Treasury directive encouraging SOEs to procure from other SOEs without a tender where applicable.

Sales and Marketing Interventions: FY2026/27

PetroSA has set a roadmap towards approximately 1.4 billion litres of sales volume for FY2026/27, with the objective of increasing volumes, recovering market share and maximising asset utilisation. The sales portfolio is being diversified across the oil industry, wholesale market, strategic customers and SOE tenders.

The Q2–Q4 commercial programme includes accelerating in-tank transfers from the Voorbaai Terminal to integrated oil companies, with a planned 120,000 m³; relaunching gasoline sales to the oil industry and independent retailers, with 90,000 m³ targeted; securing Island View Terminal offtake contracts, including TIR00, CAL001 and additional agreements, with 150,000 m³ targeted; and recovering approximately 210,000 m³ of lost wholesale market share.

Additional interventions include stock-replenishment negotiations with Eskom targeting approximately 50,000 m³ and pursuing speciality products and strategic tenders—including HFO, Transnet, Department of Defence and RT70 opportunities—targeting approximately 330,000 m³. Collectively, these initiatives are intended to improve asset utilisation, increase revenue generation, rebuild market share and strengthen long-term customer relationships.

Liquidity, Market and Supply-Side Pressures

PetroSA continues to face liquidity pressure arising from geopolitical and market conditions. The presentation notes that disruptions associated with the Russia/Ukraine war and other geopolitical developments threaten the steady supply of molecules, while disruption around the Strait of Hormuz can increase insurance, risk premiums, logistics costs and ultimately product costs.

The absence of a retail network also limits the company’s ability to optimise margins.

Product suppliers increasingly require letters of credit, prepayments and/or parent-company guarantee.

Banks, key vendors and insurers remain cautious about PetroSA’s financial position, resulting in measures such as cash collateralisation of letters of credit, tighter payment terms and challenges in renewing some insurance policies.

PetroSA is therefore continuing to rationalise payment obligations, manage its working-capital cycle and reduce its creditors book. SARS remains one of its major creditors and is being actively managed through ongoing engagement regarding the debt arrangement.

Creditor and Legal Matters

PetroSA has an outstanding SARS tax debt of approximately R3.6 billion, with approximately R1.5 billion in interest and penalties. A revised compromise proposal dated 1 September 2026 proposes a full and final settlement of R1.5 billion, comprising a R200 million upfront goodwill payment and R1.3 billion payable over 36 months, subject to SARS consideration.

Gunvor indicated an intention to institute liquidation proceedings in May 2026. The underlying debt was settled in full in August 2026, excluding interest, with R639 million funded through a shareholder loan and R157 million paid from PetroSA’s available cash resources.

On 11 September 2026, PetroSA received an application from Nako Energy (Pty) Ltd seeking provisional liquidation. The presentation records Nako’s claim at approximately R600 million, while PetroSA also records an amount of approximately R830 million owed to PetroSA by Nako. PetroSA has appointed attorneys to defend the application.

The matter is before the courts and is sub judice; PetroSA is therefore limiting substantive public comment while the legal process proceeds.

GTL Refinery Reinstatement

PetroSA remains resolute on reinstating the Mossel Bay GTL refinery to support security of supply and restore sustainable refinery operations. The refinery reinstatement business case was completed in August 2026.

A service provider has been selected for the preparation and planning phase and a service provider appointed for the feedstock-selection study. A condition assessment and feedstock study were scheduled for September 2026 as the next technical engagements.

The reinstatement assessment provides for a phased approach:

  • Phase 1 targets approximately 18,000 barrels per day at an estimated investment of R5.8 billion;
  • Phase 2 targets approximately 46,000 barrels per day at an estimated additional investment of R8.5 billion.

The programme is intended to protect the value of PetroSA’s refinery assets, restore sustainable refinery operations, create local economic opportunities and strengthen security of supply.

Commercial Diversification

PetroSA has introduced a new product suite, including jet fuel and lubricants, and has secured large jet-fuel supply contracts, including with SAA and FlySafair. The company is actively engaging SOEs to become a preferred supplier and supplier of choice.

The presentation identifies GTL reinstatement as an opportunity to strengthen the company’s position in a period of geopolitical uncertainty and elevated crude-oil prices. SANPC has also been assigned first right to supply molecules at competitive prices, strengthening the potential alignment between PetroSA’s commercial recovery and the emerging national energy champion.

Going Concern and Audit Position

Despite the financial and liquidity pressures, PetroSA has remained a going concern and has received an unqualified audit opinion over the five-year period.

The company’s strategic response is therefore focused on stabilising liquidity, reducing operating and creditor pressures, growing volumes and market share, diversifying revenue, and progressing GTL refinery reinstatement as part of a longer-term turnaround.

SANPC: Building the National Energy Champion

The operationalisation of SANPC represents a major step in consolidating strategic petroleum infrastructure and creating an integrated platform for future growth. Following Cabinet approval of the SANPC design, relevant assets, contracts and people were transitioned from the legacy entities.

SANPC was operationalised on 1 May 2025. Current priorities include stabilising the organisation, completing priority asset and contractual transitions, improving trading and wholesale margins, strengthening shared services and developing an integrated growth strategy.

CEF has identified financial, operational and strategic enablers requiring accelerated attention, including funding architecture, commercialisation of priority assets, integrated governance and stakeholder engagement, organisational capability, portfolio scope and orderly resolution of legacy challenges.

Risk-Adjusted Plan to Accelerate SANPC Value Creation

CEF is implementing a Risk-Adjusted Plan designed to unlock merger roadblocks and accelerate value realisation. The plan includes stabilising the Group and SANPC funding architecture, accelerating commercialisation and revenue ramp-up, institutionalising integrated merger governance, building a fit-for-purpose SANPC organisation and clarifying portfolio scope and phasing.

A CEF-led Value Realisation Office is being established around commercialisation, change management and project management. CEF has also secured AT Kearney to support accelerated operationalisation of the merger.

SANPC Refinery Programme: Restoring Domestic Refining Capacity

The SANPC refinery development programme responds to the decline in domestic refining capacity. The presentation noted that imported fuels account for approximately 61% of domestic fuel demand, compared with 22% in 2019.

The programme combines early revenue generation, infrastructure development and bankability, followed by refinery redevelopment after a Final Investment Decision.

Phase 1: Stabilization and Early Revenue Generation: 2026–2027

  • Storage leasing and tank commercialization.
  • Fuel blending operations.
  • Reinstatement of LPG import and distribution infrastructure.
  • Product trading and logistic services.
  • Commercial laboratory and testing services.
  • Estimated investment: US$305 million.

Phase 2: Infrastructure Development and Bankability: 2027–2028

  • Rail siding refurbishment.
  • Detailed feasibility studies.
  • Environmental and regulatory approvals.
  • Funding mobilization and strategic partnerships.
  • Treasury approvals and Final Investment Decision.
  • Estimated investment: US$45 million.

Phase 3: Refinery Redevelopment: post-Financial Investment Decision (FID)

  • Planned refinery capacity: approximately 400,000 barrels per day.
  • Throughput: approximately 18.4 million tonnes per annum.
  • Full-conversion refinery using advanced conversion technology.
  • Processing units: approximately US$4.2 billion.
  • Site infrastructure: approximately US$1.4 billion.
  • Marine and storage facilities: approximately US$0.8 billion.
  • Contingency: approximately US$0.4 billion.
  • Estimated refinery investment: US$6.8 billion.
  • Combined SANPC refinery programme investment: approximately US$7.15 billion.

The presentation emphasized that the construction would take approximately 48 months following FID, with full programme delivery over approximately six to seven years.

Redevelopment Roadmap and Potential Economic Impact

The prefeasibility work presents a three-phase roadmap: a bridge phase using imports and existing storage and transfer infrastructure; a base refinery redevelopment phase targeting approximately 400,000 barrels per day; and a potential full-scale operation with throughput of approximately 400,000 to 650,000 barrels per day.

The presentation estimates that the full-scale scenario could support approximately 16,220 jobs and contribute approximately R16 billion to GDP from refining and manufacturing, excluding temporary jobs still being confirmed in the study. The broader SANPC programme estimates approximately 12,500 construction jobs and 2,850 permanent operational jobs, subject to further technical, commercial, funding, regulatory and investment decisions.

CEF’s Priorities Going Forward

CEF’s immediate priorities are to stabilise and turn around operating entities, diversify commercial opportunities and revenue streams, accelerate SANPC through the Risk-Adjusted Plan, restore domestic refining capability and strengthen South Africa’s long-term energy security.

The Group will continue to focus on responsible stewardship of public assets, strengthened governance and internal controls, improved execution capability and transparent engagement with government, employees, industry, communities, investors and other stakeholders.

Dr Mokoka said: “The operating environment remains challenging, but it also presents an opportunity to reposition the CEF Group for sustainable growth. Our task is to stabilise what requires stabilisation, unlock the value in our strategic assets, accelerate SANPC’s development and restore refining capability in a manner that strengthens energy security and creates sustainable value for South Africa.”

CEF remains committed to the responsible and sustainable operationalisation of SANPC and to ensuring that the Group’s strategic assets and capabilities contribute to a secure, competitive and sustainable energy future.

In conclusion.

“Our financial results demonstrate the resilience of the Group and the strength of our diversified portfolio. iGas continues to deliver strong returns, SFF remains financially robust, and we remain focused on stabilising PetroSA through liquidity management, commercial recovery, revenue diversification and the reinstatement of the Mossel Bay GTL refinery, while advancing SANPC as South Africa’s future National Energy Champion.”

The acquisition of the former SAPREF refinery asset, the operationalisation of SANPC and the advancement of the refinery development programme represent important milestones in restoring domestic refining capability, strengthening energy security and supporting economic growth.

The SANPC Refinery Development Programme is not only an investment in energy infrastructure, but an investment in South Africa’s future.

CEF remains committed to strengthening governance systems, enhancing internal controls and ensuring responsible stewardship of public assets.”

For more information, contact:

Jacky Mashapu
